scenes.dialogue: A criminal court has convicted Ravi. He believes the court misunderstood the evidence.
In another case, Meera believes a lower court acted beyond its legal powers. Can both simply ask for another trial?
The law provides different remedies: appeal and revision. And choosing the correct remedy, court and deadline matters.
Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or B N S S, let us understand the difference through these two examples.
scenes.shown: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, or BNSS, let us understand the difference through these two examples.

scenes.dialogue: Section Four Thirteen says an appeal exists only where the law provides one.
scenes.shown: Section 413 says an appeal exists only where the law provides one.

scenes.dialogue: Under Section Four Fifteen, an ordinary conviction by a Magistrate generally goes to the Sessions Court.
scenes.shown: Under Section 415, an ordinary conviction by a Magistrate generally goes to the Sessions Court.

scenes.dialogue: A conviction by a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge goes to the High Court.
So Ravi's Magistrate conviction ordinarily takes him to Sessions.
But guilty pleas and petty cases have restrictions under Sections Four Sixteen and Four Seventeen.
scenes.shown: But guilty pleas and petty cases have restrictions under Sections 416 and 417.

scenes.dialogue: Always check whether the particular decision is appealable.
An appeal can challenge findings on facts and law, within the permitted scope.
Suppose Ravi says the eyewitness could not have identified him in darkness. The appellate court can examine the trial record and his grounds.
Section Four Twenty Seven allows different outcomes: dismissing the appeal, reversing the conviction, or ordering a retrial.
scenes.shown: Section 427 allows different outcomes: dismissing the appeal, reversing the conviction, or ordering a retrial.

scenes.dialogue: It may also alter the finding or the sentence, within statutory limits.
An appeal is a real opportunity to challenge the decision, but success still depends on the case.
Take ordinary conviction appeals, other than death sentences.
The usual filing period is thirty days to Sessions and sixty days to the High Court, from the sentence or order.
scenes.shown: The usual filing period is 30 days to Sessions and 60 days to the High Court, from the sentence or order.

scenes.dialogue: These periods come from Article One Fifteen of the Limitation Act, not from a general B N S S deadline.
scenes.shown: These periods come from Article 115 of the Limitation Act, not from a general BNSS deadline.

scenes.dialogue: An application for criminal revision ordinarily has ninety days, under Article One Thirty One.
scenes.shown: An application for criminal revision ordinarily has 90 days, under Article 131.

scenes.dialogue: Acquittal appeals, victim appeals, death sentences, Supreme Court proceedings and special statutes need their own limitation checks.
Count the deadline carefully. Section Twelve of the Limitation Act excludes the relevant starting day.
scenes.shown: Count the deadline carefully. Section 12 of the Limitation Act excludes the relevant starting day.

scenes.dialogue: It also excludes the time legally required to obtain specified copies.
So apply for the certified copy promptly, and preserve the dates.
If Ravi files late, Section Five allows the court to condone the delay when sufficient cause is shown.
scenes.shown: If Ravi files late, Section 5 allows the court to condone the delay when sufficient cause is shown.

scenes.dialogue: That requires the court's decision. Delay is not automatically excused simply because an appeal has been prepared or filed.
Ravi files his appeal. Does his prison sentence automatically stop? No.
Under Section Four Thirty, the appellate court may suspend execution of the sentence, giving written reasons.
scenes.shown: Under Section 430, the appellate court may suspend execution of the sentence, giving written reasons.

scenes.dialogue: It may release a confined appellant on bail or on his own bond.
For offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or ten years or more, the Public Prosecutor must first get a chance to object in writing.
scenes.shown: For offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10 years or more, the Public Prosecutor must first get a chance to object in writing.

scenes.dialogue: If Ravi was on bail and got three years or less, the trial court must grant him bail to file his appeal, unless there are special reasons.
So Ravi should seek the necessary interim order. Keep two questions separate.
Should the conviction be overturned? And should execution of the sentence be suspended while the appeal is pending?
Revision is different. Section Four Thirty Eight lets the Sessions Judge or High Court examine a lower criminal court's record.
scenes.shown: Revision is different. Section 438 lets the Sessions Judge or High Court examine a lower criminal court's record.

scenes.dialogue: It checks correctness, legality, propriety and procedural regularity.
Sections Four Forty and Four Forty Two set out the revisional powers.
scenes.shown: Sections 440 and 442 set out the revisional powers.

scenes.dialogue: Suppose Meera challenges an order because the court lacked the legal authority to make it.
If the revision is maintainable, it may address that defect.
It is a discretionary supervisory remedy, not a routine second appeal for arguing the entire evidence again.
Three limits matter. Section Four Thirty Eight bars revision against interlocutory orders.
scenes.shown: Three limits matter. Section 438 bars revision against interlocutory orders.

scenes.dialogue: The Supreme Court has explained that an order's legal character matters, not merely when it was made.
A person who chooses Sessions revision cannot then bring another revision before the High Court.
And Section Four Forty Two generally prevents a party from using revision after leaving an available appeal unfiled.
scenes.shown: And Section 442 generally prevents a party from using revision after leaving an available appeal unfiled.

scenes.dialogue: The revisional court also cannot directly turn an acquittal into a conviction.
Remember, revision is not a shortcut around appeal restrictions.
Appeals are not only for convicted persons. The proviso to Section Four Thirteen gives a victim a right of appeal.
scenes.shown: Appeals are not only for convicted persons. The proviso to Section 413 gives a victim a right of appeal.

scenes.dialogue: That covers an acquittal, conviction for a lesser offence, or inadequate compensation.
For example, an injured victim may challenge an acquittal through the appropriate appellate court.
Section Four Eighteen separately concerns government appeals against an inadequate sentence.
scenes.shown: Section 418 separately concerns government appeals against an inadequate sentence.

scenes.dialogue: And Section Four Nineteen deals with specified appeals against acquittal.
scenes.shown: And Section 419 deals with specified appeals against acquittal.

scenes.dialogue: Who is appealing, and what is being challenged, determines the route and any permission required.
One final timeline. Section Four Fifteen, sub section Four, requires certain appeals to be disposed of within six months of filing.
scenes.shown: One final timeline. Section 415(4) requires certain appeals to be disposed of within six months of filing.

scenes.dialogue: These are appeals against sentences under specified sexual offence provisions of the B N S.
scenes.shown: These are appeals against sentences under specified sexual offence provisions of the BNS.

scenes.dialogue: This is not a six month deadline for every appeal or revision.
scenes.shown: This is not a six-month deadline for every appeal or revision.

scenes.dialogue: Remember: an appeal challenges a decision within the statutory right; revision provides a narrower supervisory check.
Identify the remedy, the court and the limitation period early.
Obtain the copies, prepare clear grounds, and seek a separate interim order whenever necessary.
